All three dichlorobenzenes have the same molar mass and almost the same intermolecular
forces, so **melting** point is decided by how well the molecules **pack into a crystal** —
and packing depends on **symmetry**.
**(c) 1,4-Dichlorobenzene (para)** ✓ is the most **symmetrical**: the two chlorines lie
exactly opposite one another, so the molecule is linear and flat and the molecules stack
neatly into a compact, well-ordered lattice. Breaking that lattice needs the most energy, so
the melting point is the highest, **53 °C**.
The others are less symmetrical and pack badly:
**(b) 1,3-Dichlorobenzene (meta)** melts at **−25 °C**
**(a) 1,2-Dichlorobenzene (ortho)** melts at **−17 °C**
So the para isomer melts some seventy degrees above the other two.
The distinction between melting and boiling point is worth keeping clear, because the two
follow different rules:
**Melting point** depends on **lattice packing**, so the symmetrical para isomer wins.
**Boiling point** depends on **dipole moment** and van der Waals forces, and there the **para**
isomer is lowest, because its two C–Cl dipoles cancel exactly and it is non-polar.
The same effect explains why p-dichlorobenzene can be sold as solid mothballs while the
ortho and meta isomers are liquids at room temperature.
∴ 1,4-dichlorobenzene.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|20|Pradeep Chemistry:
The reaction converts an alkyl halide into a nitrile:
R–Br + NaCN ⟶ **R–CN** + NaBr
(The equation as printed begins 'NaBr', which is a misprint for **RBr**; the product side
makes the intention clear.)
Classify it by what attacks and what leaves.
**The attacking species is CN⁻**, the cyanide ion. It is **electron-rich** — a lone pair on
carbon, carrying a negative charge — so it is a **nucleophile**.
**The leaving group is Br⁻**, displaced from the carbon.
One group has been **substituted** for another, and the attacking species is a nucleophile,
so this is a **nucleophilic substitution** ✓ — option (b).
Why not the others:
**(a) Elimination** would remove HBr and create a C=C double bond, giving an alkene. Nothing
is added in its place here; a group is replaced.
**(c) Electrophilic substitution** is the chemistry of **aromatic** rings, where an
electron-poor species attacks an electron-rich π system. CN⁻ is electron-rich, so it cannot
be an electrophile.
**(d) Oxidation-reduction** would require a change in oxidation state at carbon; replacing Br
by CN leaves it unchanged.
This particular substitution is useful because it **lengthens the carbon chain by one**, and
the nitrile can then be hydrolysed to an acid or reduced to an amine.
∴ nucleophilic substitution reaction.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|21|Pradeep Chemistry:
Two things have to be right: the **carbon count** and the **choice of cyanide**.
**Carbon count.** Propanenitrile is CH₃CH₂–**CN**, three carbons in all. The –CN supplies
one, so the alkyl halide must supply **two**: it is **ethyl bromide**, not propyl bromide.
That eliminates (b) and (c).
**Which cyanide.** The cyanide ion is **ambident** — it can attack through either atom — and
which end attacks depends on the nature of the salt:
**KCN is ionic**, so it supplies free CN⁻. The **carbon** is the more nucleophilic end, so
the carbon attacks and the product is the **nitrile**, R–C≡N ✓
**AgCN is largely covalent**, so the carbon is tied up in the Ag–C bond and only the
**nitrogen** lone pair is free to attack. The product is the **isocyanide**, R–N≡C ✗
Since propanenitrile is wanted, the reagent must be **KCN**, which eliminates (d).
So the answer is **ethyl bromide + alcoholic KCN** ✓ — option (a):
CH₃CH₂Br + KCN ⟶ **CH₃CH₂CN** + KBr
The ambident behaviour of cyanide is worth remembering as a pair: **KCN gives the nitrile,
AgCN gives the isocyanide** — and the two products are quite different, the nitrile
hydrolysing to an acid and the isocyanide reducing to a secondary amine.
∴ ethyl bromide + alcoholic KCN.

The **nitrite ion is ambident** — it can attack through either its nitrogen or one of its
oxygens — and which end attacks depends on how ionic the metal nitrite is.
**NaNO₂ is ionic.** It supplies the free NO₂⁻ ion, in which the **oxygen** is the more
nucleophilic site. Oxygen attacks, and the product is the **alkyl nitrite**, an ester of
nitrous acid:
C₂H₅Br + NaNO₂ ⟶ **C₂H₅–O–N=O** (ethyl nitrite) + NaBr
**AgNO₂ is largely covalent.** The Ag–O bonds tie up the oxygens, leaving only the
**nitrogen** lone pair free. Nitrogen attacks, and the product is the **nitroalkane**:
C₂H₅Br + AgNO₂ ⟶ **C₂H₅–NO₂** (nitroethane) + AgBr
So in the order asked — NaNO₂ first, then AgNO₂ — the products are
**C₂H₅ONO, C₂H₅NO₂** ✓ — option (b)
Option (c) has the two **the wrong way round**, which is the intended trap.
The two products are genuinely different compounds, not isomers in name only: the nitrite is
an **ester** that hydrolyses back to the alcohol, while the nitroalkane has a **C–N bond**
and can be reduced to an amine.
The same ionic-versus-covalent rule governs the cyanides: **KCN gives the nitrile, AgCN the
isocyanide** — the identical pattern one group along.
∴ C₂H₅ONO, C₂H₅NO₂.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|25|Pradeep Chemistry:
SN1 reactivity depends on one thing above all: **how stable the carbocation is** that forms
when the halide leaves, since that ionisation is the slow step.
Classify the three bromides by the cation each would give:
**(A)** a straight-chain bromide with Br on the **end** carbon ⟹ a **primary** carbocation —
very unstable, so SN1 is essentially impossible. **Slowest**
**(C)** Br on a carbon flanked by two alkyl groups ⟹ a **secondary** carbocation —
stabilised by two +I alkyl groups. Moderate
**(B)** Br on a carbon **next to a C=C double bond** ⟹ an **allylic** carbocation. This is the
key case: the positive charge is **delocalised over two carbons** by resonance with the
double bond, so it is far more stable than an ordinary secondary cation. **Fastest** ✓
So the order is **B > C > A** ✓ — option (c).
The general ranking of carbocation stability, which this question is built on:
**allylic ≈ benzylic > tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl**
with allylic and benzylic owing their place to **resonance** rather than to induction.
It is worth noting that the SN2 order would be almost the reverse, since SN2 is fastest at
the least hindered carbon — the primary bromide A — which is why the question specifies SN1.
∴ B > C > A.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|30|Pradeep Chemistry:
**Enantiomers** are non-superimposable mirror images. Because they are mirror images, every
**scalar** physical property is identical: they have the same melting point, the same boiling
point, the same density, the same refractive index and the same solubility in ordinary
solvents.
The one property that differs is the **direction in which they rotate the plane of polarised
light** ✓ — one rotates it clockwise (dextrorotatory, **+**) and the other anticlockwise
(laevorotatory, **−**), by exactly the **same angle**.
So options (a) boiling point, (c) melting point and (d) solubility are all **the same** for a
pair of enantiomers, and only (b) distinguishes them.
The reason is symmetry: a physical property can only differ between mirror images if the
measurement itself is **chiral**. Plane-polarised light is chiral (it can be resolved into
left- and right-circularly polarised components), and so it can tell them apart. A melting
point apparatus cannot.
The same principle has a practical consequence: enantiomers **cannot be separated by
distillation or ordinary crystallisation**, since they boil and melt alike. Separation
(resolution) requires a **chiral** environment — reaction with a chiral acid or base to form
diastereomeric salts, or chromatography on a chiral column.
It also matters biologically: enzymes are chiral, so they distinguish enantiomers sharply —
one may be a medicine and the other useless or harmful.
∴ rotation of polarized light.

Bromine adds to an alkene through a cyclic **bromonium ion**, so the second bromide must
attack from the **opposite face**. The addition is therefore strictly **anti**, and the
stereochemistry of the product follows from the geometry of the starting alkene.
**trans-But-2-ene**, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ with the methyls on opposite sides. Adding Br anti across
the double bond gives **2,3-dibromobutane** in which the two stereocentres have **opposite**
configurations — (2R,3S). That molecule has an **internal mirror plane**, so it is
**achiral**: it is the **meso** compound.
Attack can occur at either carbon of the bromonium ion, and attack on either face gives the
**same** meso product — the two routes are indistinguishable. That is what option (a) means
by 'two identical mesomers' ✓
So trans-but-2-ene gives a **single, optically inactive** product.
The companion result completes the picture and shows the answer is not an accident:
**cis**-but-2-ene, treated the same way, gives the **racemic** pair (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) —
two enantiomers in equal amounts, option (b)'s answer.
So the **geometry of the alkene determines the stereochemistry of the product**: trans ⟶
meso, cis ⟶ racemic. This pair of results is the classical evidence that bromine addition is
anti and proceeds through a bridged ion rather than an open carbocation.
∴ 2 identical mesomers.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|38|Pradeep Chemistry:
Aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution, but they react readily if the ring carries
**electron-withdrawing groups ortho or para to the halogen**. The mechanism is **SNAr**: the
nucleophile adds to give a negatively charged **Meisenheimer intermediate**, and the more
that negative charge can be delocalised onto the withdrawing groups, the faster the reaction.
So count the **–NO₂ groups ortho or para to the halogen**:
**(iv)** 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene — **three** nitro groups, all ortho or para ⟹ **fastest**
**(iii)** 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene — **two** ⟹ next
**(ii)** p-nitrochlorobenzene — **one** ⟹ slower
**(i)** p-chloro-N,N-dimethylaniline — the substituent is **–NMe₂**, which **releases**
electrons. It makes the ring more electron-rich and the Meisenheimer intermediate less
stable, so the reaction is **slower than in chlorobenzene itself** ⟹ **slowest**
So the order is **iv > iii > ii > i** ✓ — option (c).
The effect is enormous, not marginal: chlorobenzene needs 300 °C and 300 atm to be converted
to phenol, while 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene (picryl chloride) hydrolyses in **warm water**.
The nitro group must be **ortho or para** for this: a **meta** nitro group withdraws only
inductively, because the negative charge of the intermediate cannot reach it by resonance,
and it has comparatively little effect.
∴ iv > iii > ii > i.

**Iodoform, CHI₃**, is a pale yellow solid with a characteristic smell, once widely used as a
wound antiseptic. Its germicidal action is **not** due to the molecule itself.
When iodoform is applied to skin or a wound, it is slowly decomposed by the air, the warmth
and the tissue, and it **liberates free iodine**:
2CHI₃ ⟶ ... ⟶ **3I₂** + other products
It is that **iodine** which is the actual germicide: it oxidises and denatures the proteins
and enzymes of the bacteria and kills them. So the antiseptic action is due to the
**liberation of I₂** ✓ — option (b).
This explains several things about iodoform in practice. Its action is **slow but
prolonged**, because the iodine is released gradually rather than all at once — which is
exactly what a dressing needs. And a sample that has lost its iodine is useless, however
much solid remains.
The same principle underlies **tincture of iodine** (iodine in alcohol) and **povidone-iodine**
(Betadine), which also work by delivering free iodine, the second one slowly from a polymer
complex.
Option (a) would require CHI₃ to be toxic to bacteria as a molecule, which it is not, and
option (c) overstates the molecule's own contribution.
∴ liberation of I₂.

**DDT** is **p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane**, the first of the modern synthetic
insecticides. Paul Müller received the Nobel Prize for discovering its insecticidal action in
1939, and it was used on an enormous scale against malarial mosquitoes and crop pests.
It is a **non-biodegradable pollutant** ✓ — option (c) — and that is the reason it was
eventually banned in most countries.
The chemistry behind the persistence is worth stating. DDT is a **chlorinated aromatic**
compound with very strong, unreactive **C–Cl bonds** and no functional group that soil
bacteria can attack. It is also **fat-soluble and almost insoluble in water**, so it is not
washed away. Its half-life in soil is measured in **years**, in some conditions more than a
decade.
The consequence is **biomagnification**. Because DDT dissolves in fat rather than water, it
accumulates in the fatty tissue of every organism that absorbs it, and its concentration
multiplies at each step up the food chain — from water to plankton to fish to birds. In birds
of prey it interfered with calcium metabolism, thinning eggshells so that they broke, and
that was what brought the problem to public attention in the 1960s.
Options (a), (b) and (d) each misdescribe it: it is not a fertiliser, it is certainly not
biodegradable, and it is not a greenhouse gas.
∴ non-biodegradable pollutant.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|31|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Boiling point depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces, and for these compounds
that means **van der Waals (dispersion) forces**, which grow with **molecular size and
mass**.
The measured values are
**1-Bromoethane** C₂H₅Br, M = 109 — **38 °C** (lowest)
**1-Bromopropane** C₃H₇Br, M = 123 — **71 °C**
**1-Bromobutane** C₄H₉Br, M = 137 — **102 °C**
**Bromobenzene** C₆H₅Br, M = 157 — **156 °C** (highest)
so in **increasing** order:
**1-Bromoethane < 1-Bromopropane < 1-Bromobutane < Bromobenzene** ✓ — option (d)
The order is simply the order of **increasing molecular mass**, which is what makes this
question quick once the masses are compared. Each extra –CH₂– adds about 30 degrees, because
it adds surface area over which the molecules can attract one another.
Bromobenzene is highest for two reasons together: it is the heaviest, and its **flat aromatic
ring** allows a large contact area between molecules, so the dispersion forces are stronger
still than mass alone would suggest.
The general rule for a homologous series: **boiling point rises steadily with chain length**,
and for isomers of the same mass it **falls** with branching, since a branched molecule is
more nearly spherical and touches its neighbours over less area.
∴ 1-bromoethane < 1-bromopropane < 1-bromobutane < bromobenzene.

Note: the printed key gives (c), which places 1-bromoethane above 1-bromobutane. Boiling
point rises with molecular mass in this series, so the key is wrong and has been corrected
to (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|42|Pradeep Chemistry:
All three reagents convert an alcohol into an alkyl halide, so the answer is **(d) all the
above** ✓. Each works on a different halide.
**(a) HCl + ZnCl₂** — the **Lucas reagent**, for alkyl **chlorides**. Zinc chloride is a Lewis
acid: it coordinates to the hydroxyl oxygen and turns –OH into a good leaving group, after
which chloride attacks.
R–OH + HCl --ZnCl₂--> R–Cl + H₂O
**(b) Red P + Br₂** — for alkyl **bromides**. The two combine in the flask to make **PBr₃**,
which is awkward to store, so it is generated in situ:
2P + 3Br₂ ⟶ 2PBr₃, then 3R–OH + PBr₃ ⟶ 3R–Br + H₃PO₃
**(c) H₂SO₄ + KI** — for alkyl **iodides**. The acid liberates HI from the iodide, and the HI
then reacts with the alcohol. (In practice **phosphoric** acid is preferred, because
concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidises some of the HI to iodine.)
So the three cover chloride, bromide and iodide respectively — which is why the question can
list them together and expect 'all of the above'.
The common thread is that **–OH is a poor leaving group**, so every method must first
convert it into something better: a protonated hydroxyl, a phosphite ester, or an oxygen
coordinated to a Lewis acid.
∴ All the above.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|5|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
HBr in **CCl₄** means no peroxide, so the addition is **ionic and Markovnikov** — and the
carbocation formed then **rearranges**, which is the point of the question.
**Step 1 — protonate the double bond.** The alkene is CH₂=CH– attached to the ring carbon
C-1, which also bears a methyl. H⁺ adds to the terminal CH₂ (the carbon with more hydrogens),
putting the positive charge on the inner carbon:
ring–C1(CH₃)–**C⁺H–CH₃**  — a **secondary** carbocation
**Step 2 — look for a rearrangement.** C-1 is **quaternary**: it carries two ring bonds, a
methyl and the side chain, so it has **no hydrogen** to donate. But it can donate a
**methyl**. A 1,2-**methyl shift** from C-1 to the cationic carbon moves the charge onto C-1:
ring–**C1⁺**–CH(CH₃)₂  — now a **tertiary** carbocation, and much more stable
**Step 3 — bromide attacks** the rearranged cation at C-1:
**1-bromo-1-isopropylcyclohexane** ✓ — the structure in option (d), with Br on the ring
carbon and an isopropyl group beside it
The distractors correspond to the steps left out:
**(a)** is the **anti-Markovnikov** product, which would need peroxide
**(c)** is the Markovnikov product **without** rearrangement
**(b)** involves a hydride shift that C-1 cannot provide
The signal to watch for is a **quaternary carbon next to the carbocation**: no hydride is
available, so if a rearrangement occurs it must be an alkyl shift.
∴ option (d).

Note: the printed key gives (a), the anti-Markovnikov primary bromide. HBr in CCl₄ without
peroxide adds by the Markovnikov route, and the secondary cation rearranges to the tertiary
one, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|7|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Ethanol at **high temperature** acts as a base and solvent rather than a nucleophile, so the
reaction is **elimination**, and with a secondary halide in a polar protic solvent it goes by
**E1** — through a carbocation that can rearrange.
The substrate, 2,2-dimethyl-3-bromobutane, is **(CH₃)₃C–CHBr–CH₃**.
**Step 1 — ionise.** Bromide leaves, giving
(CH₃)₃C–**C⁺H**–CH₃  — a **secondary** carbocation
**Step 2 — rearrange.** The neighbouring carbon is quaternary, carrying three methyls, so no
hydride is available — but a **methyl can migrate**. A 1,2-methyl shift gives
(CH₃)₂**C⁺**–CH(CH₃)₂  — a **tertiary** carbocation, far more stable
**Step 3 — eliminate.** A proton is lost from the adjacent CH, and by **Zaitsev's rule** the
more substituted alkene forms:
(CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂ = **2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene** ✓ — a tetrasubstituted alkene, the most stable
possible from this skeleton
So the answer is option (a).
The distractors mark the steps omitted:
**(b) 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene** is what you get by eliminating from the **unrearranged** cation
**(c) and (d)** are **substitution** products, which would dominate at **low** temperature
where ethanol acts as a nucleophile instead
Two signals in the question point to the answer: **'high temperature'** says elimination, and
the **quaternary carbon** beside the leaving group says rearrangement.
∴ 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

Note: the printed key gives (b), the unrearranged alkene. The secondary cation rearranges by
a methyl shift to the tertiary one before eliminating, so the key is wrong and has been
corrected to (a).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|11|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The phrase 'in presence of peroxide' is a trap, because the **peroxide effect works only
with HBr**.
The anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch) addition requires a free-radical **chain** to propagate, and
both propagation steps must be energetically favourable. Comparing the three hydrogen
halides:
**HCl** — the H–Cl bond is **too strong** (431 kJ mol⁻¹) to be broken by the carbon radical,
so that propagation step is endothermic and the chain dies
**HBr** — the H–Br bond (366 kJ mol⁻¹) is just right; both steps are exothermic and the chain
runs ✓
**HI** — the I• radical is formed easily but adds to the alkene only reluctantly, so again the
chain fails
So with **HCl the peroxide has no effect at all**, and the reaction follows the ordinary
**ionic, Markovnikov** route:
CH₃–CH=CH₂ + H⁺ ⟶ **CH₃–C⁺H–CH₃**  (the more stable **secondary** carbocation)
and the intermediate is that **carbocation**, option (b) ✓
The distractors assume the radical mechanism: **(a)** and **(c)** are free **radicals**, which
would form only if the peroxide effect operated.
The thing to carry away: the peroxide effect is a **property of HBr alone**. Seeing
'peroxide' in a question is not enough — check which halide it is before switching to the
radical mechanism.
∴ CH₃C⁺HCH₃.

Note: the printed key gives (c), a primary free radical. The peroxide effect does not operate
with HCl, so the intermediate is the secondary carbocation of the ionic route, and the key is
wrong and has been corrected to (b).
